从拉面食券机到居酒屋干杯，以客人的身份在日本点菜、订座、说明过敏、结账和道谢，吃: From the meal ticket machine at a ramen shop to a toast at an izakaya, learn to order, reserve a table, explain allergies, pay, and say thank you as a customer in Japan, so you can enjoy your meal and always say the right thing.
拉面店的食券机: The meal ticket machine at a ramen shop
周六中午，健太带リン去一家很有人气的拉面店。门口立着一台券売機（食券机），按钮上: It's Saturday around noon, and Kenta takes Lin to a popular ramen shop. By the entrance stands a 「券売機」 (meal ticket machine), and every button on it is in Japanese. After they buy their tickets and sit down at the counter, a staff member comes over to ask how firm they want their noodles and how strong they want the flavor, and whether they'd like some free rice.
拉面店的店员，二十多岁，嗓门大，忙得团团转但很热情: Staff member at the ramen shop; in his twenties, loud-voiced and rushed off his feet, but very friendly
在东京IT公司工作第二年的中国人，爱吃，日语还在练，遇事会鼓起勇气开口: Chinese woman in her second year at an IT company in Tokyo; loves food, is still working on her Japanese, and works up the courage to speak up when something comes up
リン在语言交换认识的日本朋友，二十多岁，美食控，熟悉各种小店: Japanese friend Lin met through a language exchange; in his twenties, a foodie who knows all kinds of little local places
リン和健太是朋友，用普通体聊天，很放松。店员对客人用接客敬语（いらっしゃいませ、: Lin and Kenta are friends and chat in plain (casual) style, completely relaxed. The staff member uses customer-service keigo with customers (「いらっしゃいませ」, 「かしこまりました」). Lin is the customer, so polite です/ます style is all she needs with the staff. She doesn't need to be especially humble, but she shouldn't talk to them like a friend either.
这家要先买餐券哦。: You buy a meal ticket first here, you know.
「〜んだよ」是朋友之间解释情况的口气，带点“告诉你哦”的感觉。对店员或长辈说就显: 「〜んだよ」 is how friends explain a situation to each other, with a "just so you know" feel. Said to a staff member or someone older, it can sound like you're lecturing them; switch to 「〜んです」 to be polite.
诶，按哪个好？全是日语……: Huh, which one am I supposed to press? It's all in Japanese...
左上那个大按钮是最受欢迎的拉面。加料在下面那排。: The big button in the top left is the most popular ramen. Toppings are on the bottom row.
券売機有个小规律：左上角、按钮最大的通常是招牌菜。看不懂的时候先按它，基本不会错: There's a handy rule of thumb for meal ticket machines: the biggest button, in the top-left corner, is usually the house specialty. If you can't read anything, press that one first and you basically can't go wrong.
那我要这个，再加个溏心蛋。钱是从这里塞进去吧。: Okay, I'll get this one and a seasoned egg. And the money goes in here, right?
欢迎光临！食券我收下了。面的硬度、口味浓淡、油量，有什么偏好吗？: Welcome! I'll take your tickets. Any preferences for the firmness of the noodles, the strength of the flavor, or the amount of oil?
「お預かりします」是店员收东西时的固定说法，意思是“先替您保管”。这是店员一方的: 「お預かりします」 is the set phrase staff use when they take something from you; it means "I'll hold on to this for you." It's customer-service language for the staff's side, so customers don't say it themselves.
不好意思，我是第一次来，有推荐的吗？: Excuse me, it's my first time here. Do you have any recommendations?
先坦白「初めてなんですが」，店员马上就知道该怎么照顾你。比假装懂、结果点错要好得: If you admit up front 「初めてなんですが」 (it's my first time), the staff will know right away how to look after you. That's much better than pretending you know what you're doing and ending up ordering the wrong thing.
第一次的话，推荐全部选“普通”！: For first-timers, we recommend "regular" for everything!
那就只把面做硬一点，麻烦了。: Then just the noodles on the firm side, please.
「〜めで」表示“偏……一点”：硬め、柔らかめ、濃いめ、少なめ。后面接「お願いしま: 「〜めで」 means "a bit on the ... side": 硬め (firmer), 柔らかめ (softer), 濃いめ (stronger), 少なめ (less). Add 「お願いします」 after it and you have a complete, polite order.
面偏硬，其他普通，对吧。米饭是免费的，要吗？: Firm noodles, everything else regular. Rice is free. Would you like some?
这里的「大丈夫です」是“不用了”的委婉拒绝。只说「いりません」太硬，后面加一句「: Here, 「大丈夫です」 is a gentle way of saying "no, thank you." Saying only 「いりません」 is too blunt; add 「ありがとうございます」 after it, and you've graciously acknowledged their kind offer.
我全部要浓一点。米饭也要。: I'll have everything on the strong side. And rice too, please.
吃完以后把碗放到吧台上，再用抹布擦一下就好。: When you're done eating, put your bowl up on the counter and give the counter in front of you a quick wipe with the cloth.
多谢款待！很好吃。: Thank you for the meal! It was delicious.
谢谢光临！欢迎再来！: Thank you very much! Please come again!
「食券を買う」买餐券；坐下后把食券放在吧台上交给店员: 「食券を買う」 to buy a meal ticket; after you sit down, put the ticket on the counter to hand it to the staff
拉面店、立食荞麦面店常见，现在很多也能刷交通卡: Common at ramen shops and stand-up soba shops; many now also take transit IC cards
「麺の硬さ」面的硬度；「麺大盛り」面加量: 「麺の硬さ」 noodle firmness; 「麺大盛り」 extra noodles
反义是「柔らかめ」；博多拉面还有「バリカタ」「ハリガネ」等更硬的叫法: The opposite is 「柔らかめ」; Hakata ramen also has words for even firmer noodles, such as 「バリカタ」 and 「ハリガネ」
反义「薄め」。家系拉面会问「味の濃さ」: The opposite is 「薄め」. Iekei ramen shops ask about 「味の濃さ」 (flavor strength)
不知道怎么选时说「全部普通で」最稳: When you don't know what to choose, 「全部普通で」 is the safest thing to say
「味付け玉子」的简称，拉面最受欢迎的加料之一: Short for 「味付け玉子」; one of the most popular ramen toppings
叉烧、海苔、葱等，「トッピングを追加する」: Chashu pork, nori, green onions, and so on; 「トッピングを追加する」 to add a topping
「大盛り無料」的店不少；吃不完就别点，剩下店员会难过: Plenty of shops offer 「大盛り無料」 (free large portions); if you can't finish it, don't order it, since leftovers make the staff sad
主要是博多拉面的说法，汤留着再加一份面: Mainly a Hakata ramen term: you keep your soup and get another serving of noodles in it
吃完「丼をカウンターに上げる」是很多拉面店的小礼貌: Putting your bowl up on the counter when you finish (「丼をカウンターに上げる」) is a small courtesy at many ramen shops
「カウンター席」吧台座位；一个人吃饭也很自在: 「カウンター席」 counter seat; it's comfortable even when you're eating alone
请做得偏……一点: please make it a bit on the ... side
形容词词干 + め + でお願いします（硬め・少なめ・濃いめ）: Adjective stem + め + でお願いします (硬め, 少なめ, 濃いめ)
不是“要很硬”，而是“在标准基础上稍微调一点”，语气很温和，店员也好拿捏。点拉面: It doesn't mean "make it really firm"; it means "adjust it slightly from the standard," so it sounds very gentle, and it's easy for the staff to get right. You can use it when ordering ramen, rice bowls, or coffee. It's the most natural way for a customer to adjust a dish to their taste.
初めてなんですが + 想问的事: 初めてなんですが + what you want to ask
「〜んですが」先交代背景，再提问，听的人马上知道你需要帮助。日本店员很喜欢被这样: 「〜んですが」 gives the background first and then asks the question, so the listener knows right away that you need help. Japanese staff really like being asked this way: they get to use what they know to help you, which makes them much happier than watching you quietly order the wrong thing and end up disappointed.
我第一次来，怎么点单呢？: It's my first time here. How do I order?
我第一次来，推荐哪个？: It's my first time here. Which one do you recommend?
名词 + は大丈夫です（+ ありがとうございます）: Noun + は大丈夫です (+ ありがとうございます)
日本人不太说「いりません」，因为听起来像在推开对方的好意。「大丈夫です」意思是“: Japanese people don't often say 「いりません」, because it sounds like pushing away the other person's kindness. 「大丈夫です」 means "I'm fine as I am," which makes the refusal very soft. But pair it with a little wave of the hand or a smile; otherwise it can sometimes be mistaken for "yes, that's fine."
水不用了，谢谢。: I'm fine without water. Thank you.
第一次去拉面店、看不懂规则时，先说「初めてなんですが」；点单时用「〜めでお願いし: When you go to a ramen shop for the first time and don't understand how things work, start with 「初めてなんですが」. When ordering, adjust the flavor with 「〜めでお願いします」. Turn down things you don't want gently with 「大丈夫です」.
不要不买食券就直接坐下喊“我要一碗”，店员只能停下手里的活来解释。也别学店员说「: Don't sit down without buying a meal ticket and call out "One bowl, please!" The staff will have to stop what they're doing to explain. And don't copy the staff by saying 「お預かりします」 or 「かしこまりました」. Those are phrases for the staff's side, and they sound strange coming from a customer.
店员听到「初めてなんですが」会觉得被信任，愿意多照顾你；吃完把碗放上吧台、说一声: When the staff hear 「初めてなんですが」, they feel trusted and are happy to take extra care of you. When you put your bowl up on the counter after eating and say 「ごちそうさまでした」, the people in the kitchen feel their hard work has been noticed, and they'll remember you next time.
拉面店吧台后面常常只有一两个人，又煮面又切叉烧又收碗。食券制就是为了让他们少碰钱: Behind the counter of a ramen shop there are often only one or two people, boiling noodles, slicing chashu pork, and clearing bowls all at once. The meal ticket system exists so they have to handle money less and can concentrate on making noodles. So when you finish, putting your bowl up on the counter and wiping your spot with the cloth may take only ten seconds, but it genuinely lightens their load. When you leave, say 「ごちそうさまでした」 toward the kitchen, and the sweat-drenched staff will look up and call back 「ありがとうございました！」. That little exchange is what trust between a customer and a shop looks like. And if you don't understand something, ask. Don't be afraid of looking silly. A first-timer who bravely asks is far more welcome than one who pretends to know.
店员问「麺の硬さはどうしますか」，你第一次来不知道选什么，最合适的回答是？: The staff member asks 「麺の硬さはどうしますか」. It's your first time and you don't know what to choose. What's the best answer?
先说明自己是第一次，再请对方推荐，既礼貌又能得到最合适的选择。「かしこまりました: Explain that it's your first time and ask them for a recommendation. It's polite, and it gets you the best choice. 「かしこまりました」 is a staff phrase; customers don't say it.
店员问要不要免费米饭，你不想要。哪句最自然？: The staff member asks if you'd like free rice, but you don't want any. Which is the most natural?
「大丈夫です」加一句道谢，是日本人拒绝好意时最常用、最柔和的说法。: 「大丈夫です」 plus a thank-you is the most common and gentlest way Japanese people turn down an offer.
想让面条稍微硬一点，应该怎么说？: You want your noodles a little firmer. What should you say?
「〜めでお願いします」表示在标准上稍微调整，是客人点单的固定说法。: 「〜めでお願いします」 means a slight adjustment from the standard; it's the set phrase customers use when ordering.
